title: Ordinary Hecke Specht Polytabloids and Signed Murphy Comparison

items.title: Hecke row permutation modules and ordinary Dipper-James polytabloids
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$, $n\ge0$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant commutation, standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-involution $T_i^*=T_i$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). All modules are right modules. Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse of the left action of [[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]].

For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S_\lambda$ be its row (Young) subgroup, let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled $\lambda$-tableau, let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, let $D_\lambda=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}$ be the set of minimal-length right coset representatives, and let $w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$. Put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$, and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is $P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid generator.

The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ defined on the distinguished family $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by $\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}$; the **DJ form** is its restriction to $P(\lambda)$. For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set $x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that $M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form. Every base change $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, produces all objects over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers below prove that the distinguished families and the form are base-change compatible. Empty shapes and the cases $n=0,1$ are included. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A definition item that fixes the normalizations; the mathematical structure is supplied by the later items of this page. The elements $x_\lambda,y_\lambda,w_\lambda$ and the modules $M(\lambda),P(\lambda)$ are the Dipper-James conventions exactly as indexed in Fayers, 'An algorithm for semistandardising homomorphisms' (author version), §2.1: $x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in W_\lambda}T_w$, $y_\lambda=\sum_{w\in W_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w$, $w_\lambda$ determined by $t^\lambda w_\lambda=t_\lambda$, $M^\lambda=x_\lambda H_n$, $S^\lambda=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'}H_n$. Fayers's field hypothesis and parameter name are immaterial: the formulas are polynomial and define the objects after every base change in which $q$ is invertible. The dictionary between Fayers's right tableau action $t\mapsto tw$ and the library's left action $\sigma\cdot t$ is $t\cdot\sigma=\sigma^{-1}\cdot t$, and under it $D_\lambda$ and $w_\lambda$ agree. Heard-Kujawa, arXiv:2207.00654, §2.2-§2.5, carries the same combinatorial generator $z_\lambda=x_\lambda T_{\sigma_\lambda}y_{\lambda^{\mathsf T}}$ (their $\sigma_\lambda$ is this $w_\lambda$) and the same standard-basis indexing by standard tableaux of the transposed shape (their (2.5.1), which quotes the Dipper-James basis theorem [DJ86, Theorem 5.6]). Their Hecke normalization is the symmetric one $(T_i-q)(T_i+q^{-1})=0$ with $x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}q^{\ell(w)}T_w$, so HK supply the combinatorial shape of the construction, not the exact coefficients, which are fixed here in the $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$ normalization. Definitional scope: the permutation form is fixed here by its values on the distinguished free family proved in [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]; it is a chosen contravariant form and the historical DJ self-form on $S^\lambda$ is its restriction, not an additional source claim. No choice principle is used.

items.title: The row permutation module: distinguished basis and Hecke action
items.statement:
In the notation of [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every commutative $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;
2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;
3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$
4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change $R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Direct transcription of the standard row-module facts from the two independent treatments read for this page. Mathas, manuscript, §3: Lemma 3.2 gives $m_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\lambda$ for $w\in S_\lambda$; Proposition 3.3 gives that $D_\lambda$ is a set of right coset representatives with $\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$ for $w\in S_\lambda$, $d\in D_\lambda$; Corollary 3.4 shows that $M_\lambda$ is free on the family $m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ and proves exactly the three-case formula displayed in (3). Ryom-Hansen, arXiv:0904.4243v5, §2, equations (5)-(6), states the same basis and the same action rules for $x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$ in the same normalization. The left identities in (2) follow from the right ones by $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$ and $\ell(w^{-1})=\ell(w)$. Part (4) is immediate because all structure constants are Laurent polynomials in $q$. The verification of (3) in the sources is the coset bookkeeping of Mathas §3. This item does not assert the cell law or the polytabloid basis; those are separate suppliers on this page. No choice principle is used.

items.title: The permutation form is H-contravariant and restricts to the DJ form
items.statement:
In the notation of [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every commutative $R$ and $q\in R^\times$, the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ is well defined, symmetric and $R$-bilinear, with $\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}$ on the distinguished basis of [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]. It is $H$-contravariant:
$$\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)\qquad(x,y\in M(\lambda),\ h\in H).$$
Its restriction $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ to the polytabloid module $P(\lambda)$ satisfies the same identity for $x,y\in P(\lambda)$ and is called the DJ form. Both $\beta$ and $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ are compatible with every base change $R\to R'$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: The distinguished row basis is proved free, so the diagonal weights $q^{\ell(d)}$ define the stated symmetric bilinear form. For each generator $T_i$, the row tabloids split into singleton orbits (same row, action scalar $q$) and two-element swap orbits. Order a swap pair with the shorter representative first. Its right-action matrix is $A_i=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\q&q-1\end{pmatrix}$ and its Gram matrix is $D=\operatorname{diag}(q^a,q^{a+1})$. Direct multiplication gives $A_iD=DA_i^{\mathsf T}$; singleton blocks satisfy the same equality, and different blocks are orthogonal. Thus $\beta(xT_i,y)=\beta(x,yT_i)$ for all row-module vectors. Iteration over a generator word, reversing the word on the second side, gives $\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)$ for every $h$. Restriction to the actual submodule $P(\lambda)$ is contravariant. All coordinates and structure constants are universal Laurent polynomials, so the whole proof survives arbitrary base change. Nondegeneracy of the restricted form is not asserted and no choice is used.

items.title: The Hecke sign automorphism, pullback and contragredient dual
items.statement:
For every commutative $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive $R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with $\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.
2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying $R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$ is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.
3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with $(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and $(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.
4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit $q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
The quadratic relation gives $T_i^{-1}=q^{-1}(T_i-(q-1))$, so $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$. Inverses satisfy the braid and distant-commutation relations, so their uniform scalar multiples do too; the quadratic relation is preserved by interchanging its roots $q,-1$. Applying $\theta$ twice fixes every generator. Hence it is an involutive algebra automorphism, and it commutes with star because both constructions fix the reversed generator relations. On a reduced word, $\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$. All these formulas are universal and survive base change.
For pullback, $\theta$ is onto, so a subspace or submodule is stable for the new action exactly when it was stable for the old action. The same underlying inclusion and quotient maps prove exactness, all submodule/radical/simple and composition-series claims, and twisting twice is identity. The action $(f\cdot h)(m)=f(mh^*)$ satisfies $((f\cdot h)\cdot k)(m)=f(mk^*h^*)=f(m(hk)^*)$. For finite free modules, the dual basis identifies base changes, and commuting $\theta$ with star proves $(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.
To compute $\theta(x_\lambda)$ without any generic semisimplicity, use its left $-1$ eigenvalue for each parabolic generator: $T_i\theta(x_\lambda)=\theta(((q-1)-T_i)x_\lambda)=-\theta(x_\lambda)$. If $a=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}a_wT_w$ is such a common eigenvector, pairing $w,s_iw$ with $\ell(s_iw)=\ell(w)+1$ in the standard multiplication formula gives $qa_{s_iw}=-a_w$. Thus $a_w=(-q)^{-\ell(w)}a_1$ by a finite reduced word; the common eigenspace is the free line $Ry_\lambda$ over every ring, without dividing by $q+1$ or a quantum factorial. For the longest parabolic word $w_0$ of length $N$, expand each product $\theta(T_w)=\prod_j((q-1)-T_{i_j})$. Its unique top-length standard term is $(-1)^{\ell(w)}T_w$; any omitted letter has fewer factors and cannot create length $N$. Consequently the coefficient of $T_{w_0}$ in $\theta(x_\lambda)$ is $(-1)^N$. In $cy_\lambda$ it is $c(-q)^{-N}$, so $c=q^N$, using only this unit. Thus $\theta(x_\lambda)=q^Ny_\lambda$ and applying $\theta$ again gives $\theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-N}x_\lambda$. At $q=1$, $T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}=T_w$, so $\theta(T_w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}T_w$: it is sign pullback, not inversion of the permutation. Empty and singleton cases have $N=0$. No choice principle is used.

items.title: Row symmetrizers and signed column symmetrizers vanish outside dominance
items.statement:
For every commutative ring $R$, unit $q$ and partitions $\alpha,
u\vdash n$, if $\alpha$ is not dominated by $
u'$, then $x_\alpha H y_
u=0$. The vanishing is a universal Laurent-polynomial identity, remains valid at singular parameters and uses no cancellation of $q+1$. The proof explicitly sorts parabolic double cosets and uses the zero product $(1+T_i)(1-q^{-1}T_i)=0$. Empty shapes and $n=0,1$ are included. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
**Lemma.** For partitions λ,ν, if λ is not dominated by ν', then xλ H yν=0 over every R.

Decompose permutations into minimal `(Sλ,Sν)` double-coset representatives d. The standard length-additive double-coset decomposition reduces xλH yν to the products xλT_d yν: left Sλ factors act on xλ by powers of q and right Sν factors act on yν by powers of −1. To justify the needed double-coset facts directly, sort the images of each right block and the inverse images of each left block; the resulting unique minimal representative is increasing within each block in both directions. Its block-incidence matrix a_ij counts the positions of right block j sent to left block i. Each nonempty intersection block is contiguous within the two corresponding blocks: the simultaneous increasing orders place the entries grouped by the other block in consecutive order. Consequently Sλ∩dSνd^{-1} is a standard parabolic subgroup inside Sλ, generated by adjacent transpositions of these contiguous intersections; its conjugate inside Sν is likewise standard. This also gives the usual length-additive transversal fact by counting inversions inside and between the blocks.

The incidence matrix has row sums λ_i and column sums ν_j. If all a_ij≤1, then for every k, Σ_{i≤k}λ_i≤Σ_j min(k,ν_j)=Σ_{i≤k}ν'_i. Thus the hypothesis forces an intersection block of size at least2. Choose its adjacent generators s in Sλ and t in Sν with sd=dt; minimality gives ell(sd)=ell(d)+1=ell(dt), hence T_sT_d=T_dT_t. Factor xλ=X(1+T_s) by minimal right representatives of <s> in Sλ and yν=(1-q^{-1}T_t)Y by minimal left representatives of <t> in Sν. These factorizations follow by pairing the length-additive standard-basis terms in the defining sums, including their (-q)^{-ell} weights. Therefore

xλT_dyν=X T_d(1+T_t)(1-q^{-1}T_t)Y=0,

because `(1+T_t)(1-q^{-1}T_t)=0` follows exactly from the quadratic relation. No division or cancellation of q+1 occurs. This proves the lemma.

items.title: The Murphy cellular basis, the cell law and the Murphy form
items.statement:
For every commutative $R$, $q\in R^\times$, and $\lambda\vdash n$ with its row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put $m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an $R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.
2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$ (dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.
3. The **Murphy cell module** $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.
4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with $m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is symmetric, associative in the sense $G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.
5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank $f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
# Standalone integral Murphy cellular basis and form

Same author/run/construction scope as `constructive-proof.md`. This is a research-only complete proof candidate for the formerly sketch-only NEW50 premise. Source actually read: Mathas manuscript PDF objects27–36, printed18–27, in `/tmp/b50/sources/mathas_raw_pages.json`; its printed21–25 Garnir/lex basis proof is reconstructed below. The dominance upgrade here is a new trace argument using the already proved local opposite-dominance double-coset zero, rather than importing Mathas Proposition3.16 or a source20 prototype.

## Required independent published/local premises

Published IDs whose actual statements were read:

- `def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra` and `thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra`: standard basis, quadratic and braid relations, inversion length, multiplication rule. The standard-basis theorem is published; its current carrier has a judge stamp rather than a delegated audit. This is disclosed, not upgraded here.
- `def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape` and `def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition`: partitions, row/standard tableaux, conjugation.
- `cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers`: Σλ(f^λ)^2=n! for every n≥0, including the empty shape. Published independent source is `thm-robinson-schensted-correspondence`, not source20.

Local elementary prerequisites proved here or in companion `constructive-proof.md`: row-permutation-module basis/action; sign automorphism θ; minimal parabolic and double-coset sorting; opposite-dominance zero xκHyρ=0 when κ is not dominated by ρ'. None uses the Murphy basis. Thus the proposed dependency graph has no cycle: double-coset zero → this Murphy lemma → DJ split basis → comparison/form theorems.

Use A=Z[q,q^{-1}], arbitrary specialization to R, n≥0, right modules, xα=Σw∈SαT_w for compositions α. For row-standard α-tableaux s,t set m_st^α=T_dα(s)^* xα T_dα(t). The involution star fixes generators and reverses products. For partitions, use lexicographic order temporarily; dominance replaces it in Section6. Empty and singleton shapes have x=1, one tableau, H=R and all claims below reduce to multiplication in R.

## 1. Row modules and elementary ordering facts

Sorting labels inside each row gives one representative dα(t) per right coset Sαd; inversion counting gives ell(ad)=ell(a)+ell(d) for a∈Sα. Pairing terms w and ws_i in xα gives xαT_i=qxα for every adjacent generator inside Sα. Thus b_t=xαT_dα(t) form a basis of xαH: each expands with disjoint standard-basis support Sαd, with coefficient1 at T_d. The right action is q b_t if i,i+1 lie in the same row, b_{ts_i} if the swapped tableau is row-standard and its length increases, and q b_{ts_i}+(q−1)b_t if length decreases. These assertions also follow immediately by row sorting and the standard Hecke multiplication rule. The left counterparts follow by star.

For row-standard tableaux define t≥u if every initial-label row composition of t dominates that of u. We need the following elementary support lemma: if v>g, d(t)=d(g)w and ell(d(t))=ell(d(g))+ell(w), then b_vT_w has support strictly more dominant than t. No Bruhat theorem is needed. Choose a reduced word for w; the successive tableaux starting at g and ending at t are row-standard. Indeed each length-increasing adjacent-label interchange adds one inverted pair of row-reading nodes and removes none; a within-row inversion could never disappear before the final tableau t, which has none. Thus each step is an increasing-length row-standard swap s→s'=s s_i, with i in an upper row a and i+1 in a lower row b>a; s' is less dominant than s.

For any r≥s, both row tabloids r and r s_i dominate s'. Only the label cutoff m=i needs checking. For row cutoffs k<a, use `count_{≤i}(r s_i;first k rows)≥count_{≤i−1}(r;first k rows)≥count_{≤i−1}(s;first k rows)=count_{≤i}(s';first k rows)`. For k≥b use `count_{≤i}(r s_i;first k rows)≥count_{≤i+1}(r;first k rows)−1≥count_{≤i+1}(s;first k rows)−1=count_{≤i}(s';first k rows)`. For a≤k<b use the first bound again, since s' contains neither label i at that cutoff and `count_{≤i}(s')=count_{≤i−1}(s)`. items.title: Theta transports the Murphy cellular structure to the signed cell modules
items.statement:
Let $\theta$ be the involutive automorphism of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $m_{st}$, $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, $G_\lambda$ be as in [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]. Then:

1. $\theta(m_{st})=\theta(T_{d(s)}^*)\theta(m_\lambda)\theta(T_{d(t)})$ with $\theta(m_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda$; $\{\theta(m^{\mu}_{st}):\mu\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is again an $R$-basis of $H$; the spans $\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})$ and $\theta(I^{\unrhd\lambda})$ of the $\theta$-images of the corresponding basis elements are two-sided ideals of $H$ (images of two-sided ideals under the automorphism $\theta$), and $(\{\theta(m_{st})\},\unrhd)$ is again a cellular basis with the same dominance poset, whose ideal filtration is the $\theta$-image of the original one. The image ideals are in general \emph{different} subspaces from the originals: already for $n=2$, $\lambda=(2)$ one has $\theta(x_{(2)})=q-T_1\notin R(1+T_1)=I^{\unrhd(2)}$. The poset is preserved; the ideal subspaces are not, in general.
2. $\theta$ induces an isomorphism of right $H$-modules $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta\xrightarrow{\sim}\theta(M(\lambda))/(\theta(M(\lambda))\cap\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda}))$, $m_t\mapsto\theta(m_t)$, whose target is the cell module of the transported basis; in particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ is free of rank $f^\lambda$ with basis $\{\theta(m_t):t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.
3. The transported form $G_\lambda^\theta(x,y):=G_\lambda(\theta^{-1}x,\theta^{-1}y)$ is the Murphy form of the transported basis; it is symmetric, is associative for the twisted action $G_\lambda^\theta(x\cdot h,y)=G_\lambda^\theta(x,y\cdot h^*)$ and has the same radical, so the assignment $x\mapsto\theta^{-1}x$ identifies the twisted cell module with the cell module for the same underlying $H$-form.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is free of rank $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ and carries the transported form $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Because $\theta$ is an involutive $R$-algebra automorphism commuting with star, its image of the FULL Murphy basis (all partition shapes) is again a basis, and it transports the cellular involution and coefficient-independent multiplication congruences with image ideals $\theta(I^{\unrhd\lambda})$ and $\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})$. These image ideals are spans of the corresponding transported shapes and are two-sided; they need not equal the original ideals. For $n=2$, $\theta(1+T_1)=q-T_1$ is not in $A(1+T_1)$, by comparison of the two standard coefficients. The explicit basis formula follows by applying $\theta$ to all factors of $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$, using $\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda$. On the domain $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$, the map $x\mapsto\theta(x)$ obeys $\theta(x\cdot h)=\theta(x\theta(h))=\theta(x)h$ and hence is an actual module isomorphism to the transported cell row. Define its image form by $G_{\rm image}(\theta(x),\theta(y))=G(x,y)$. Associativity follows from $G(x\theta(h),y)=G(x,y\theta(h)^*)=G(x,y\theta(h^*))$, which is exactly the transported relation with ordinary target action. Symmetry and the image radical follow from the same invertible coordinate map. The form is the transported cellular multiplication coefficient since applying $\theta$ preserves that scalar. This separates domain pullback from target transported row, includes every shape, and uses no generic identification, choice or old convention. All identities survive base change.

items.title: Murphy cells are the same-shape contragredient Specht duals
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. 3. All statements are compatible with every base change $A\to R$, $v\mapsto q$; the construction uses no generic semisimplicity, no nondegeneracy of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ and no choice principle.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^\times$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with its standard basis, star anti-involution, the modules $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H\supseteq P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the distinguished basis $\{b_r=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}\}$ of $M(\lambda)$ and the permutation form $\beta$, the Murphy basis $\{m^\rho_{st}\}$, the dominance ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with basis $\{m_s\}$ and the Murphy form $G_\lambda$.

[F1] The trace $\tau\colon H\to R$, $\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$, satisfies $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ and $\tau(a^*b)=B_0(a,b)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ for standard basis elements $a=T_u$, $b=T_v$; the bilinear form $\tau(a^*b)$ has unit diagonal in the standard basis ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F2] $M(\lambda)$ is free on $\{b_r\}$, $\beta(b_r,b_v)=\delta_{r,v}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}$, and $\beta$ is $H$-contravariant; $P(\lambda)$ is free on $\{e_t=z_\lambda T_{d_\lambda'(t)}\}$ and a split direct summand of $M(\lambda)$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]], [[lem-dj-bridge-permutation-form-invariance-and-restriction]], [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]).

[F3] $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$, $K:=M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is the kernel of the quotient, $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the Murphy elements $m^\nu_{uv}$ with $\nu\rhd\lambda$, and $\{m_s\}$ is an $R$-basis of the cell module ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] $x_\kappa Hy_\rho=0$ whenever $\sum_{i\le k}\kappa_i>\sum_{i\le k}\rho'_i$ for some $k\ge1$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-parabolic-double-coset-annihilation]]).

[F5] The star-contragredient $N^\circ=\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,R)$ of a right $H$-module is a right $H$-module via $(fh)(m)=f(mh^*)$; for finite free $N$ it is finite free of the same rank and $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The correctly scaled universal trace formula.** Work first over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using $q=v$ as the formal parameter. For $d,e\in D_\lambda$, length additivity gives $b_d=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}T_{ud}$, and [F1] gives $\tau(b_d^*b_e)=0$ when $d\ne e$, while $\tau(b_d^*b_d)=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}q^{\ell(ud)}=q^{\ell(d)}P_\lambda(q)$, where $P_\lambda(q):=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}q^{\ell(u)}$. By bilinearity, $$\tau(a^*b)=P_\lambda(q)\,\beta(a,b)\qquad(a,b\in M_A(\lambda)).$$ The factor $P_\lambda$ is essential; it is not generally a unit and can vanish after specialization. It is nonzero in the domain $A$, since its constant coefficient is $1$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 **Orthogonality before specialization.** Put $K_A=M_A(\lambda)\cap I_A^{\rhd\lambda}$ and $p=z_\lambda h$. For a higher Murphy element $m^\nu_{uv}=T_{d_\nu(u)}^*x_\nu T_{d_\nu(v)}$ with $\nu\rhd\lambda$, its product with $p$ after star is $$ (m^\nu_{uv})^*p=T_{d_\nu(v)}^*x_\nu\bigl(T_{d_\nu(u)}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\bigr)y_{\lambda'}h=0,$$ because $x_\nu Hy_{\lambda'}=0$ by [F4]. The outer factor multiplies a zero vector; no factor is silently discarded. Expand $k\in K_A$ in the higher Murphy basis using [F3]. Then $k^*p=0$ and step 1.1 gives $P_\lambda(q)\beta(k,p)=0$. Cancel this nonzero polynomial only in the universal domain $A$, proving $\beta(K_A,P_A)=0$. The quotient and its kernel in [F3] are base-change compatible: the quotient is free on the supplied standard basis, its kernel is the split kernel of that quotient, and the independent Murphy construction identifies its specialization with $M_R(\lambda)\cap I_R^{\rhd\lambda}$. Thus tensoring the zero pairing identity gives $\beta(K_R,P_R)=0$ for every $R$ and unit $q$. No cancellation is performed in $R$, including when $P_\lambda(q)=0$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 **The descended pairing is perfect.** Define $B_\lambda(a+K_R,p)=\beta(a,p)$; step 2.1 proves this is well defined. Contravariance gives $B_\lambda(ch,p)=B_\lambda(c,ph^*)$, so its adjoint $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ is an $H$-homomorphism by [F5]. The map $M(\lambda)\to M(\lambda)^\circ$, $a\mapsto\beta(a,-)$, is an isomorphism with unit diagonal $q^{\ell(d)}$. Compose this map itself with restriction $M(\lambda)^\circ\to P(\lambda)^\circ$, which is onto because $P(\lambda)$ is split in $M(\lambda)$. The resulting surjection kills $K_R$ and therefore factors onto $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$. Both are free of rank $f^\lambda$. Choosing preimages of their finitely many basis vectors gives a right inverse of its square matrix; the determinant is a unit, so the adjoint is an isomorphism. This proves clause 1 without any nondegeneracy of the DJ self-form. [step 2.1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

4.1 **Kernel, finite formulas and every base change.** The kernel of $M(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ is $P(\lambda)^\perp$ by its definition. Since the factored adjoint is an isomorphism, this is exactly $K_R=M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$. Write $e_t=\sum_d a_{d,t}b_d$ with the finite Laurent-polynomial coefficients of the integral polytabloid basis. Then $B_\lambda(m_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d_\lambda(s))}a_{d_\lambda(s),t}$. Compute these coefficients by the finite signed-symmetrizer expansion and standard-basis multiplication; the inverse pairing matrix is $\det(B_\lambda)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(B_\lambda)$. Over $A$ its determinant is a Laurent unit by step 3.1, so both the pairing and its inverse specialize to every $R$, retaining perfectness and the kernel identity. Empty shapes have the rank-one pairing $1$. No generic semisimplicity, nondegeneracy of the DJ self-form, division by a specialized Poincaré polynomial or choice principle is used. items.title: Ordinary Specht modules are the signed conjugate Murphy cells
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

[F6] $J(A)$ is nilpotent and $A/J(A)$ is semisimple for a finite-dimensional algebra over a field ([[thm-jacobson-radical-is-nilpotent-and-the-quotient-is-semisimple]]).

[F7] The kernel of the quotient $M(\lambda')\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ is $P(\lambda')^\perp$, and $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda')^\circ$ under the same-shape pairing ([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]]).

[F8] Base change: all structure constants lie in $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ and specialize along $v\mapsto q$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The approved integral map.** Identify $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta$ with $\theta(M(\mu))/\theta(K_\mu)$, where $K_\mu=M(\mu)\cap I^{\rhd\mu}$. By [F2], literal left multiplication by $q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}$ kills $\theta(K_\mu)$ and induces the surjection $F:C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta\to P(\lambda)$ sending the class of $x_\mu$ to $z_\lambda$. In particular $F(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$ for any row-module lift, independently of that lift. Both modules are free of rank $f^\mu=f^\lambda$; finite basis preimages give a right inverse of the square matrix of $F$, so its determinant is a unit and $F$ is an isomorphism. Set $\Phi_\lambda=F^{-1}$. Its $H$-linearity with the twisted target action gives $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)$, where this expression uses the ordinary action on the underlying Murphy module. All these matrices and their inverses lie in the universal Laurent ring and specialize by [F8]. [F1, F2, F4, F8, algebra]

2.1 **Generic uniqueness of the forms, after the integral isomorphism.** Work over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with formal $q=v$ and $K=\mathbb Q(v)$. The matrix of the regular trace form $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_K(L_{ab})$ has Laurent-polynomial entries. At $v=1$ its matrix is $n!$ times the permutation matrix $u\leftrightarrow u^{-1}$: in the regular group basis left multiplication by a nonidentity group element has trace zero, whereas the identity has trace $n!$. Its determinant is therefore nonzero, so the regular trace form is nonsingular over $K$. If $a\in J(H_K)$, every $ab$ is nilpotent by [F6], and $L_{ab}$ has trace zero; nondegeneracy forces $a=0$, so $H_K$ is semisimple. Each cellular layer is an ideal in a quotient of this semisimple algebra, with multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=G_\mu(b,c)a\otimes d$. If $G_\mu$ had a nonzero radical, $(\operatorname{rad}G_\mu)\otimes C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)$ would be a nonzero square-zero ideal of that quotient, stable under its surrounding algebra by the cell law and contravariance, a contradiction. Thus $G_\mu$ is nonsingular, and the cellular rank-one operators realize the full matrix algebra on $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)_K$. Every module endomorphism is scalar because it commutes with all matrix units; this conclusion also holds on the $\theta$-twist, since $\theta(H_K)=H_K$. On that twist, any contravariant form $B'$ defines an operator $U$ by $G_\mu^\theta(Ux,y)=B'(x,y)$. Contravariance and nonsingularity imply that $U$ commutes with the module action, so $B'$ is a scalar multiple of $G_\mu^\theta$. No generic argument was used to establish the integral map or basis. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **The exact generator computation.** The expansion in [F2] has distinct distinguished row-module vectors and length $L+\ell(u)$, so [F3] gives $$\beta(z_\lambda,z_\lambda)=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}q^{-2\ell(u)}q^{L+\ell(u)}=q^L\sum_{u\in S_\mu}q^{-\ell(u)}=q^{L-N}P_\mu(q).$$ The last equality pairs $u$ with $w_0(S_\mu)u$. By [F4], $G_\mu(m_0,m_0)=P_\mu(q)$. Therefore, with the specified normalization $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0$, the only possible comparison unit is $u_\lambda(q)=q^{N-L}$. This computation uses the distinguished-basis definition of $\beta$, not any incorrectly unscaled trace identity. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **Universal form identity.** Transfer the DJ form to $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta$ using $F=\Phi_\lambda^{-1}$: set $B'(c,d)=\beta(Fc,Fd)$. This is contravariant for the twisted action, as is $G_\mu^\theta$. Both are nonzero over $K$, since their respective generator values are $q^{L-N}P_\mu(q)$ and $P_\mu(q)$, nonzero in that field. Step 2.1 makes them proportional, and step 2.2 determines the scalar as $q^{N-L}$, proving $G_\mu^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=q^{N-L}\beta(x,y)$ over $K$. Both sides have matrices in $A$; the injection $A\to K$ proves their equality already in $A$, and then [F8] specializes it to every commutative $R$ with unit parameter. No cancellation of $P_\mu(q)$ takes place after specialization. [F3, F4, F5, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 **Radicals, divisibility, quotients and duality.** The unit form identity and the isomorphism $\Phi_\lambda$ identify the form radicals and yield $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including zero quotients. Over a field, a vector outside a nonzero cell-form radical generates its whole cell module: choose a vector pairing to $1$ and use its finite basis expansion in the cell rank-one action $x m_{uv}=G_\mu(x,m_u)m_v$. Thus every proper submodule lies in that radical, making it the unique maximal submodule and the nonzero form quotient the simple head; transfer this conclusion through $\Phi_\lambda$. If the form is identically zero only the zero form quotient is asserted, not a zero actual head. Over a PID with chosen prime $\pi$, the submodules $\{x:\beta(x,P(\lambda))\subseteq\pi^iR\}$ for every $i\ge0$ are identified with their Murphy counterparts because the forms differ by a unit; their reductions correspond as well. Applying step 1.1 to $\lambda'$ gives $P(\lambda')\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$. Compose with the same-shape perfect pairing [F7] and the commuting of star dual with $\theta$ in [F1] to obtain $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$. Empty shapes have $N=L=0$, $\Phi=1$ and unit $1$. This proves all clauses, using generic semisimplicity only for uniqueness of forms on an already integral module. No choice principle is used. [F1, F4, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the isomorphism $\Phi_\lambda$ and the exact unit identity of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]. Then:

1. For every commutative ring $R$ and $q=1$, the module $P(\lambda)$ identifies with the ordinary integral-polytabloid Specht module $R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ of [[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], with the classical left action converted to a right action by $x\cdot w=w^{-1}x$: the basis $\{e_t=z_\lambda T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)}\}$ specializes to the standard polytabloid basis and the DJ form to the standard tabloid form. The sign automorphism $\theta$ becomes the pullback along the sign twist $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$. Over every field $F$, this specialization is compatible with the conjugate-sign dictionary of [[lem-conjugate-specht-sign-duality-over-fields]].

2. For a field $F$, a unit $q\in F^\times$ and partitions $\mu,\lambda\vdash n$ with $D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$ one has $[P(\lambda):D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$, and the simultaneous sign-automorphism pullback is the same $\theta$ on both sides: $(D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta\cong D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$.

3. Suppose a Schur-algebra corner is already proved to send the Weyl module $W(\lambda)$ to $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and its head $L(\lambda)$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Then that corner gives $F(W(\lambda'))\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ and $F(L(\lambda'))\cong(D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta$, including the zero case; this is the $\theta$-twisted conjugate dictionary, never the untwisted conjugate-dual identity. No Schur-algebra theorem and no source-20 convention is a prerequisite of this conditional dictionary.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ or a commutative ring $R$ with a unit $q$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the module $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its basis $\{e_t\}$, its DJ form and its form quotient $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with basis $\{m_t\}$ and form quotient $D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$, the sign automorphism $\theta$, and the isomorphism and unit identity of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]].

[F1] $\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is an $H$-module isomorphism with $G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)$ and $u_\lambda(q)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F2] $\theta$ is the involutive sign automorphism; the twist $M^\theta$ has action $m\cdot h=m\theta(h)$, is exact, preserves composition multiplicities and maps simple modules to simple modules; at $q=1$ over a field, $\theta$ is the pullback along $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).

[F3] $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ has the standard polytabloids as a $\mathbb Z$-basis and is base-change compatible: for every commutative ring $R$ the canonical map $R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\to R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ is injective onto the span of the polytabloids in the tabloid module, and the standard polytabloids form an $R$-basis of the image ([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]]).

[F4] The conjugate-sign dictionary $S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong(S^{\lambda'}_F)^*$ holds over every field, with the explicit sign-twisted tabloid homomorphism ([[lem-conjugate-specht-sign-duality-over-fields]]).

[F5] The Hecke algebra has presentation $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant commutation, with standard basis $(T_w)_w$; $S_n$ has the Coxeter presentation $s_i^2=1$ with the same braid and distant commutation relations ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]]). The row-module and polytabloid bases are split and compatible with every coefficient-ring base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]], [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]).

[F6] The Murphy cell law and the cell form are defined by formulas with coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ and commute with base change; the independent same-shape perfect pairing gives $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)\cong P(\rho)^\circ$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]]).





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The group algebra over every coefficient ring.** Let $R$ be any commutative ring and specialize at $q=1$. The Hecke relations become $T_i^2=1$, braid and distant commutation. The Coxeter presentation in [F5] therefore gives the homomorphism $H_{R,1}(S_n)\to R[S_n]$ carrying $T_i$ to $s_i$. A reduced word shows that it carries every $T_w$ to $w$. These are bases of the source and target over $R$, so the map is an isomorphism over $R$, including in positive characteristic and with zero divisors. Equivalently the assignment $s_i\mapsto T_i$ gives its inverse directly from the presentation. No complex-field specialization, dimension comparison over a field or semisimplicity is used. [F5, algebra]

1.2 **Multiplicities and zero quotients.** For a field and unit $q$, the unit form identity in [F1] identifies $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ with $(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including zero quotients. A nonzero cell-form quotient is simple: the cell rank-one action shows that every vector outside its radical generates the cell module, so the radical is its unique maximal submodule. Thus when $D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$, the module $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ is a legitimate simple composition-factor label. Applying the exact twist equivalence in [F2] to a composition series and using [F1] gives $$[P(\lambda):D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta:D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):(D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}].$$ This proves clause 2. If a form is identically zero, only its zero form quotient is asserted; no claim is made that the actual module head vanishes. [F1, F2, F6, algebra]

2.1 **The actual polytabloids and the forms.** Give the classical tabloid module the right action $\{t\}\cdot w=\{w^{-1}\cdot t\}=\{t\cdot w\}$. The map $b_d=x_\lambda T_d\mapsto\{t^\lambda\cdot d\}$ sends the distinguished basis to the tabloid basis. It respects the right action: at $q=1$ the row-module multiplication rule is simply the permutation of these cosets, with a same-row transposition acting as $1$. Every diagonal value of $\beta$ becomes $1$, so this is an isometry to the orthonormal tabloid form. The column group of the column-filled tableau $t_\lambda$ is exactly $S_{\lambda'}$, because its columns carry the consecutive row blocks of $\lambda'$. Hence $z_\lambda=x_\lambda w_\lambda\sum_{u\in S_{\lambda'}}\operatorname{sgn}(u)u$ maps to $\sum_u\operatorname{sgn}(u)\{t_\lambda\cdot u\}$, the classical column polytabloid of $t_\lambda$ (replace $u$ by $u^{-1}$ to compare with the left-action formula). Covariance shows $e_t=z_\lambda d_{\lambda'}(t)$ maps to the polytabloid of $t_\lambda\cdot d_{\lambda'}(t)=t'$, the transpose of the standard $\lambda'$-tableau $t$. Thus the actual standard bases correspond bijectively. By the split integral classical basis in [F3] and the split Hecke basis in [F5], this identifies $P(\lambda)$ with $R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ over every $R$, and the restricted DJ form with the restricted tabloid form. [F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **The exact position of the twist.** At $q=1$, [F2] gives $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$, hence $\theta(w)=\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$. Therefore the right module $P(\lambda)^\theta$ is the sign tensor twist. Applying the involution $\theta$ to [F1] yields $$P(\lambda)^\theta\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'),$$ without a remaining twist on the Murphy cell. Combining this with the independent same-shape pairing in [F6] gives $P(\lambda)^\theta\cong P(\lambda')^\circ$. Under step 2.1, star dual is the ordinary group contragredient dual, so this is exactly the module identity $S_F^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong(S_F^{\lambda'})^*$ of [F4] after converting the published left modules to right modules. This asserts the same compatible module dictionary, not an unproved equality of separately normalized explicit maps. In characteristic $2$ the sign becomes trivial at $q=1$; conjugation remains part of the identity. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **Conditional Schur dictionary and conclusion.** Under the stated separate hypothesis on a Schur corner, its images at $\lambda'$ are $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and $D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$. The untwisted Murphy identities from step 3.1 and [F1], valid for arbitrary unit $q$ by involutivity of $\theta$, identify these with $P(\lambda)^\theta$ and $(D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta$, including the zero quotient. This proves clause 3 without a Schur theorem as a prerequisite. The actual nonzero Schur head and the Hecke cell-form quotient are distinct notions when the corner kills the former. For the empty shape, the generators, forms, twists and all isomorphisms have value $1$. All bases, maps and scalar identities are explicit and use no choice principle. [F1, F2, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

items.statement:
**Refuted claim:** the same-shape duality $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]] may be applied without a sign twist, i.e. one may conclude $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ directly.

This is false. Over $\mathbb Q$ at $q=1$ and $n=3$ the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ is the sign module, in which $T_i$ acts by $-1$, while the ordinary polytabloid module $P((3))$ and its contragredient dual are trivial, in which $T_i$ acts by $+1$. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ without $\theta$ fails in general. The correct bridge is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]; combining it with same-shape duality gives $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$, which is a different formula. No choice principle is used.

## Statement refuted

**Refuted claim:** the same-shape duality $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]] may be applied without a sign twist, i.e. one may conclude $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ directly.

This is false. Over $\mathbb Q$ at $q=1$ and $n=3$ the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ is the sign module, in which $T_i$ acts by $-1$, while the ordinary polytabloid module $P((3))$ and its contragredient dual are trivial, in which $T_i$ acts by $+1$. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ without $\theta$ fails in general. The correct bridge is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]; combining it with same-shape duality gives $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$, which is a different formula. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $\mathbb Q$, the specialization $q=1$ of the type-$A$ Hecke algebra $H$, the polytabloid module $P((3))=z_{(3)}H$ with its DJ form, the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ with its form, and the comparison theorem [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] together with its corollary [[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]].

[F1] At $q=1$ the specialization of $H$ is the group algebra $\mathbb Q[S_3]$ and the sign automorphism $\theta$ is the pullback along $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$; the partitions $(3)$ and $(1^3)$ are conjugate ([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).

[F2] The comparison theorem gives $P((3))\cong C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ with the exact unit $u_{(3)}=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{(1^3)}))-\ell(w_{(3)})}$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F3] $P((3))=x_{(3)}H$ is spanned by $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$, and $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$; the contragredient dual of a one-dimensional module with trivial action is trivial ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F4] In $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ one has $f^{(1^3)}=1$, the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$ contains the elements $1+T_i$, and the cell form has value $G_{(1^3)}(m_0,m_0)=1$ ([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).



## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The ordinary module is trivial.** At $q=1$ one has $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and $x_{(3)}T_i=\sum_wT_wT_i=\sum_wT_{ws_i}=x_{(3)}$ for each generator, because right multiplication by $s_i$ permutes the group and every $T_{ws_i}$ is again one of the summed basis elements; with the scalar carried along this reads $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}=x_{(3)}$ at $q=1$, and $P((3))=x_{(3)}H=\mathbb Q\,x_{(3)}$ is one-dimensional. Its dual is therefore also one-dimensional with trivial action. [F3, algebra]

1.2 **The cell is sign.** At $q=1$ the element $1+T_i$ lies in the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, because $1+T_1=x_{(2,1)}$ belongs to that two-sided ideal and conjugation by the invertible braid word $T_1T_2$ sends $T_1$ to $T_2$, so $1+T_2$ also belongs to it; hence in the one-dimensional cell $m_0(1+T_i)=0$, that is, $m_0T_i=-m_0$. The cell form value is $1$, and the module is the sign module. [F4, algebra]

2.1 **No untwisted isomorphism.** A right $H$-module isomorphism $f\colon C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))\to P((3))^\circ$ would satisfy $f(mh)=f(m)h$ for every $h$; taking $h=T_i$ and a nonzero $m$ gives $f(-m)=f(m)$ because $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ has $T_i$ acting by $-1$ and $P((3))^\circ$ has $T_i$ acting by $+1$, while $f(-m)=-f(m)$ in characteristic zero, so $-f(m)=f(m)$ forces $f(m)=0$, contradicting injectivity over $\mathbb Q$. Therefore no such isomorphism exists and the untwisted claim is false. The twisted statement is consistent: on $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator $T_i$ acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$, that is by $+1$, matching $P((3))$, and the unit is $u_{(3)}=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

items.title: The row and column Specht conventions in rank three
items.statement: Let $H=H_{A,q}(S_3)$, $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, and put $p_3(q)=(1+q)(1+q+q^2)$. All four modules $P((3)),P((1^3)),C_{\mathrm M}((3)),C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ have rank $1$. These identities specialize over every commutative ring with a unit parameter. No choice principle is used.

## Example

Let $H=H_{A,q}(S_3)$, $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, and put $p_3(q)=(1+q)(1+q+q^2)$. All four modules $P((3)),P((1^3)),C_{\mathrm M}((3)),C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ have rank $1$. On $P((3))$ and $C_{\mathrm M}((3))$ both generators act by $q$; on $P((1^3))$ and $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ both act by $-1$. In the canonical generators $x_{(3)}$, $y_{(3)}$, $c_{(3)}$, $c_{(1^3)}$ the respective self-form values are $1$, $q^{-3}p_3(q)$, $p_3(q)$, $1$. Thus $\Phi_{(3)}(x_{(3)})=c_{(1^3)}$ has exact form multiplier $u_{(3)}=1$, whereas $\Phi_{(1^3)}(y_{(3)})=c_{(3)}$ has $u_{(1^3)}=q^3$. In both targets the action is twisted by $\theta$, so the two module identities match. At $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the respective form values are $1,6,6,1$, and $\theta$ exchanges trivial and sign. These identities specialize over every commutative ring with a unit parameter. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The type-$A$ Hecke algebra $H$ of $S_3$ over $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ with generators $T_1,T_2$, the shapes $(3)$ and $(1^3)=(3)'$, their row and polytabloid modules and Murphy cells, the sign automorphism $\theta$ with $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$, and the comparison theorem and its corollary [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]].

[F1] $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ spans $P((3))=x_{(3)}H$ and $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$; the distinguished basis of $M((3))$ is $\{x_{(3)}\}$ with $\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$; the Murphy cell $C_{\mathrm M}((3))$ has one basis class $c_{(3)}=x_{(3)}+I^{\rhd(3)}$ and $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=P_{(3)}(q)=p_3(q)$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F2] $x_{(1^3)}=1$, $y_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w$ spans $P((1^3))=y_{(3)}H$ and $y_{(3)}T_i=-y_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$; the distinguished basis of $M((1^3))$ is the standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and $\beta(y_{(3)},y_{(3)})=q^{-3}p_3(q)$; the Murphy cell $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ has one basis class $c_{(1^3)}=1+I^{\rhd(1^3)}$ with $G_{(1^3)}(c_{(1^3)},c_{(1^3)})=1$ and $T_i$ acting by $-1$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).

[F3] The comparison theorem gives base-change compatible isomorphisms $\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ with $G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)$ and $u_\lambda(q)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}$, where the twisted action is $m\cdot h=m\theta(h)$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F4] At $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the specialization is the group algebra $\mathbb Q[S_3]$ and $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$ is the sign automorphism ([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]). The $H$-linearity of the comparison maps is supplied by [F3]; their self-form comparison is a separate assertion.



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Shape (3).** For the one-row shape, $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and pairing $u$ and $us_i$ with $\ell(us_i)=\ell(u)+1$ gives $(T_u+T_{us_i})T_i=q(T_u+T_{us_i})$, hence $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$; since $z_{(3)}=x_{(3)}T_{w_{(3)}}y_{(1^3)}=x_{(3)}$ (here $w_{(3)}=1$ and $y_{(1^3)}=1$) the module $P((3))$ is the free rank-one module on $x_{(3)}$ with action $q$. Squaring gives $x_{(3)}^2=\sum_{v,w}T_vT_w=\sum_vT_vx_{(3)}=\bigl(\sum_vq^{\ell(v)}\bigr)x_{(3)}=p_3(q)x_{(3)}$, because the length distribution in $S_3$ is $(1,2,2,1)$ and $1+2q+2q^2+q^3=(1+q)(1+q+q^2)$; hence the Murphy cell has form value $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=p_3(q)$ and action $q$, and $\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$ by [F1]. [F1, algebra]

1.2 **Shape (1^3).** For the one-column shape, $x_{(1^3)}=1$ and $P((1^3))=y_{(3)}H$ with $y_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w$. For each pair $u,us_i$ with $\ell(us_i)=\ell(u)+1$, its contribution is $a(T_u-q^{-1}T_{us_i})$, where $a=(-q)^{-\ell(u)}$. The quadratic relation gives $(T_u-q^{-1}T_{us_i})T_i=T_{us_i}-q^{-1}((q-1)T_{us_i}+qT_u)=-(T_u-q^{-1}T_{us_i})$. Summing the pairs gives $y_{(3)}T_i=-y_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$, the sign representation of the rank-one module. The distinguished basis of $M((1^3))$ is the standard basis and $\beta$ is diagonal with entries $q^{\ell(w)}$, so $\beta(y_{(3)},y_{(3)})=\sum_wq^{-2\ell(w)}q^{\ell(w)}=\sum_wq^{-\ell(w)}=q^{-3}p_3(q)$, the last equality by $w\mapsto w_0w$. Modulo the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, which contains $1+T_i$ because $1+T_1=x_{(2,1)}$ is a higher Murphy element and conjugation by the invertible braid word $T_1T_2$ sends $T_1$ to $T_2$, placing $1+T_2$ in the same two-sided ideal, the class $c_{(1^3)}$ satisfies $T_i=-1$ and $G_{(1^3)}(c_{(1^3)},c_{(1^3)})=P_{(1^3)}(q)=1$ by [F2]. [F2, algebra]

2.1 **The comparison maps.** By [F3] applied to $\lambda=(3)$, where $\lambda'=(1^3)$ and $\ell(w_0(S_{(1^3)}))=\ell(w_{(3)})=0$, the isomorphism $\Phi_{(3)}$ has unit $u_{(3)}=1$ and the identity $G^\theta_{(1^3)}(\Phi_{(3)}x_{(3)},\Phi_{(3)}x_{(3)})=\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$ is consistent because both sides are the value of the respective rank-one forms; explicitly $\Phi_{(3)}(x_{(3)})=c_{(1^3)}$ by [F3]. Applying it to $\lambda=(1^3)$, where $\lambda'=(3)$ and $\ell(w_0(S_{(3)}))=3$, $\ell(w_{(1^3)})=0$, gives $u_{(1^3)}=q^3$, and the identity $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=q^3\,q^{-3}p_3(q)=p_3(q)$ is consistent; explicitly $\Phi_{(1^3)}(y_{(3)})=c_{(3)}$. In the target $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$, hence by $(q-1)-(-1)=q$ for every unit parameter; at $q=1$ this is $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$ and scalar $+1$; in the target $C_{\mathrm M}((3))^\theta$ it acts by the ordinary action of $(q-1)-T_i$ on the class acting by $q$, hence by $(q-1)-q=-1$; these match the source actions $q$ on $P((3))$ and $-1$ on $P((1^3))$ computed in steps 1.1 and 1.2. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F3, algebra]

3.1 **Specialization and conclusion.** At $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the four form values become $1$, $1^{-3}p_3(1)=6$, $6$ and $1$, and $\theta$ is the sign automorphism exchanging the trivial and sign modules, in agreement with [F4]; the module actions match as in step 2.1. Every displayed identity is an identity in $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ between Laurent polynomials, so all of them specialize along any ring map $A\to R$ with $q\mapsto q\in R^\times$. Only the rank-one computations, the trace-free form evaluations and the comparison theorem were used; no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, F4] ∎

items.title: The two-tableau pairing at a singular parameter
items.statement: For $\lambda=(2,1)$ put $x=1+T_1$ and $b_0=x$, $b_1=xT_2$, $b_2=xT_2T_1$ in the row permutation module. Its form is $\operatorname{diag}(1,q,q^2)$ and its generator action matrices, with coordinate row vectors, are $R_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&q&q-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $R_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1&0\\q&q-1&0\\0&0&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The ordinary polytabloid basis is $p_0=z=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)=b_1-q^{-1}b_2$ and $p_1=zT_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2$. Their embedding has unit determinant on its $b_0,b_2$ coordinates, and their form is $$B=\begin{pmatrix}q+1&q^2\\q^2&q^3+q\end{pmatrix}.$$ In the Murphy quotient let $c_0=x$, $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher shape $(3)$. Its form and generator action matrices, with coordinate row vectors, are $$G=\begin{pmatrix}q+1&-1\\-1&q^2+1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_1=\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\q&q-1\end{pmatrix}.$$ On the ordinary basis the matrices are $P_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\-q^2&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $P_2=M_2$. The map $\Phi(p_0)=c_0$, $\Phi(p_1)=(q-1)c_0-c_1$ has matrix $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\q-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; it satisfies $P_iA=A((q-1)I-M_i)$ and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$. The same-shape perfect cross-pairing on the bases $(c_0,c_1)$ and $(p_0,p_1)$ has matrix $Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&q\\q&q(q-1)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $-q^2$, a unit; its entries are the row-form coefficients before quotienting. Thus the exact self-form multiplier is $1$. Both Gram determinants equal $q(1+q+q^2)$. At $q=-1$ over characteristic zero these forms are nonsingular with determinant $-1$, even though $[2]_q=0$; at $q=1$ in characteristic $2$ both reduce to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and have radical $0$. This distinguishes a singular algebra parameter from degeneracy of this particular module form. No choice principle is used.

## Example

For $\lambda=(2,1)$ put $x=1+T_1$ and $b_0=x$, $b_1=xT_2$, $b_2=xT_2T_1$ in the row permutation module. Its form is $\operatorname{diag}(1,q,q^2)$ and its generator action matrices, with coordinate row vectors, are $R_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&q&q-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $R_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1&0\\q&q-1&0\\0&0&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The ordinary polytabloid basis is $p_0=z=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)=b_1-q^{-1}b_2$ and $p_1=zT_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2$. Their embedding has unit determinant on its $b_0,b_2$ coordinates, and their form is $$B=\begin{pmatrix}q+1&q^2\\q^2&q^3+q\end{pmatrix}.$$ In the Murphy quotient let $c_0=x$, $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher shape $(3)$. Its form and generator action matrices, with coordinate row vectors, are $$G=\begin{pmatrix}q+1&-1\\-1&q^2+1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_1=\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\q&q-1\end{pmatrix}.$$ On the ordinary basis the matrices are $P_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\-q^2&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $P_2=M_2$. The map $\Phi(p_0)=c_0$, $\Phi(p_1)=(q-1)c_0-c_1$ has matrix $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\q-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; it satisfies $P_iA=A((q-1)I-M_i)$ and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$. The same-shape perfect cross-pairing on the bases $(c_0,c_1)$ and $(p_0,p_1)$ has matrix $Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&q\\q&q(q-1)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $-q^2$, a unit; its entries are the row-form coefficients before quotienting. Thus the exact self-form multiplier is $1$. Both Gram determinants equal $q(1+q+q^2)$. At $q=-1$ over characteristic zero these forms are nonsingular with determinant $-1$, even though $[2]_q=0$; at $q=1$ in characteristic $2$ both reduce to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and have radical $0$. This distinguishes a singular algebra parameter from degeneracy of this particular module form. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_3)$ over a commutative ring $R$ with $q\in R^\times$, the shape $\lambda=(2,1)=\lambda'$, the row module $M(\lambda)$ with $x=x_\lambda=1+T_1$ and the distinguished basis $\{b_0,b_1,b_2\}$, the polytabloid module $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with $z_\lambda=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)$, the permutation form $\beta$ and the Murphy cell $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with classes $c_0,c_1$ and form $G$, together with the comparison theorem and the perfect cross-pairing of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] and [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]].

[F1] $H$ has generators $T_1,T_2$ with $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid relation $T_1T_2T_1=T_2T_1T_2$ and standard basis $\{T_w\}$; $xT_1=q\,x$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]).

[F2] The distinguished basis $\{b_0,b_1,b_2\}=\{x,xT_{s_2},xT_{s_2s_1}\}$ of $M(\lambda)$ satisfies $\beta(b_i,b_j)=\delta_{ij}q^{i}$ and is the row basis of $D_\lambda=\{1,s_2,s_2s_1\}$ ([[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]).

[F3] $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ has basis $c_t=xT_{d(t)}$ for the standard tableaux $t$, and its form satisfies $m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G(c_s,c_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; the ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ contains $x_{(3)}=b_0+b_1+b_2$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] $\Phi\colon P(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ is an isomorphism with $\Phi(z)=c_0$ and unit $u_\lambda(q)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}=q^{1-1}=1$ for $\lambda=(2,1)$; the pairing $B_\lambda(m_s,p)=\beta(xT_{d(s)},p)$ is perfect with the explicit entries $B_\lambda(c_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d(s))}a_{d(s),t}$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]]).



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Row module.** From [F1], $b_0T_1=xT_1=qx=q\,b_0$, $b_1T_1=xT_2T_1=b_2$ and $b_2T_1=xT_2T_1^2=xT_2((q-1)T_1+q)=(q-1)b_2+q\,b_1$; also $b_0T_2=b_1$, $b_1T_2=xT_2^2=x((q-1)T_2+q)=(q-1)b_1+q\,b_0$ and $b_2T_2=xT_2T_1T_2=xT_1T_2T_1=q\,xT_2T_1=q\,b_2$, using the braid relation. In the basis $(b_0,b_1,b_2)$ with coordinate row vectors these are exactly the matrices $R_1$ and $R_2$ of the statement, and $\beta(b_i,b_i)=q^{i}$ by [F2] because $\ell(1)=0$, $\ell(s_2)=1$, $\ell(s_2s_1)=2$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 **Polytabloids and their form.** Since $z_\lambda=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)$ by [F4] and $y_{\lambda'}=1-q^{-1}T_1$, the displayed expressions $p_0=b_1-q^{-1}b_2$ and $p_1=zT_2=b_1T_2-q^{-1}b_2T_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2$ follow from step 1.1. Their coordinates on $(b_0,b_2)$ give the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-q^{-1}\\q&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $q\cdot q^{-1}=1$, a unit over every $R$; hence the two polytabloids span a free rank-two split submodule. The row action gives $p_0T_1=-p_0$, $p_1T_1=-q^2p_0+qp_1$, $p_0T_2=p_1$ and $p_1T_2=qp_0+(q-1)p_1$. Thus their span is stable, has precisely the displayed matrices $P_1,P_2$, and equals $zH$ because it contains $z=p_0$ and $zT_2=p_1$. Weighted inner products against the diagonal form of [F2] give $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q+1&q^2\\q^2&q^3+q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$: explicitly $B_{00}=q+q^{-2}\cdot q^2=q+1$, $B_{01}=q(q-1)+(-q^{-1})(-1)q^2=q(q-1)+q=q^2$, and $B_{11}=q^2+(q-1)^2q+q^2=q^3+q$. Its determinant is $q(q^2+q+1)$. [step 1.1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.2 **The Murphy quotient.** In $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ the higher vector $x_{(3)}=b_0+b_1+b_2$ vanishes by [F3], so $b_2=-c_0-c_1$ and $c_1=xT_2=b_1$. Then $c_0T_1=qx=q\,c_0$ and $c_1T_1=b_2=-c_0-c_1$, giving $M_1$; also $c_0T_2=c_1$ and $c_1T_2=(q-1)b_1+qb_0=(q-1)c_1+qc_0$, giving $M_2$. The defining products of [F3] give $x^2=(q+1)x$ and $xT_2x=b_1+b_2=x_{(3)}-x\equiv-x$. Also $xT_2^2x=(q-1)xT_2x+qx^2\equiv(q^2+1)x$. Reading the coefficient of $m_{t_0t_0}=x$ therefore gives $G(c_0,c_0)=q+1$, $G(c_0,c_1)=-1$ and $G(c_1,c_1)=q^2+1$; equivalently $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q+1&-1\\-1&q^2+1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $q^3+q^2+q$. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

3.1 **Comparison, cross-pairing and specializations.** The comparison theorem of [F4] gives $\Phi(z)=c_0$, hence $\Phi(p_1)=\Phi(zT_2)=c_0\theta(T_2)=(q-1)c_0-c_1$ and $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\q-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; direct matrix multiplication verifies $P_iA=A((q-1)I-M_i)$ for $i=1,2$ and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$, the latter being the form identity with the unit $u_\lambda=1$. The cross-pairing entries $B_\lambda(c_s,p_t)=\beta(b_{d(s)},p_t)$ on the standard bases give $Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&q\\q&q(q-1)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $\det Q=-q^2\in A^\times$, so the pairing is perfect as in [F4]. The two Gram determinants agree with $q(1+q+q^2)$. At $q=-1$ in characteristic zero, $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&-2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ have determinant $-1$, although $[2]_q=1+q=0$; at $q=1$ in characteristic $2$, both reduce to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $1$, hence with zero radical. All identities are Laurent-polynomial identities, so they specialize to every $R$; no choice principle is used. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F4, algebra] ∎
